newsitem.title: USA: Fran moving across Atlantic, toward U.S. coast.
newsitem.headline: Fran moving across Atlantic, toward U.S. coast.

text.p: Hurricane watches were posted in the Bahamas on Tuesday, as Hurricane Fran slowly gained strength and edged across the Atlantic toward the Florida coast, the National Hurricane Center said.

At 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT), Fran was near latitude 24.9 north and longitude 71.6 west, or about 365 miles (590 km) east of Nassau, Bahamas, and moving west-northwest near 12 mph (19 kmh), a path that forecasters said could bring the storm to the United States' southeast coast on Thursday.

Although the storm was several hundred miles (kms) east of the Florida coast, at a latitude just south of Miami, forecasters said they were expecting a gradual turn toward the northwest during the next 24 hours, diminishing Fran's threat to the heavily populated southern portion of the state.

"If this (northwest turn) actually is realized, which we think it will, it will lessen the chances of landfall in the southern Florida region and increase the chances in the north Florida to the North Carolina region, and that would be two to three days out," said Bill Frederick, a meteorologist at the National Hurricane Center.

Fran's maximum sustained winds had increased slightly to 85 mph (137 kmh), making Fran a Category 1 hurricane, and forecasters said further strengthening expected by mid-day on Wednesday would bring Fran close to Category 2 status.
"We're expecting some more intensification as the storm continues getting over warmer waters," Frederick said.

Tropical storm warnings and hurricane watches were up for much of the Bahamas by mid-day on Tuesday. A hurricane watch, indicating hurricane conditions -- maximum sustained winds of 74 mph (119 km) or higher -- would arrive within 36 hours, was in effect for the central and northwestern Bahamas from Acklins Island northwestward.

A tropical storm warning, indicating that winds of 39 to 73 mph (63-117 kph) were due within 24 hours, was in effect for the central Bahamas from Acklins Island to Cat Island. The government of the Bahamas said it would issue a hurricane warning for the northwest Bahamas as of 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Tuesday.
No storm watches or warnings were expected for the U.S. coast before Wednesday, with any threat to the coast coming later if the northwestward track materializes as expected.
Emergency workers from southern Florida north, many of them fresh off preparations for Hurricane Edouard, which churned east of the U.S. Atlantic coast last weekend, were on the alert.

"Depending upon the speed of the storm, we're looking to meet sometime Thursday afternoon. If it starts to make funny changes, we're going to meet sooner," said Clarence Skinner, head of the emergency control group in Dare County, North Carolina, noting that Fran would only get stronger as it moved over warm ocean waters.
"There's a high probability of it being a Category 3 when it comes to shore," he said.

In Dare County, which encompasses Cape Hatteras on North Carolina's Outer Banks, "no swimming" advisories were lifted at beaches on Tuesday for the first time since Edouard threatened the state late last week.
Edouard was declared extra-tropical before dawn on Tuesday as it moved in the north Atlantic southwest of Halifax, Nova Scotia.
